slides.title: A Hidden World Below
slides.kicker: Mountains and valleys hide right below the waves!
bullets: Just as land has mountains, valleys and plains, the ocean floor also has many landforms.
These underwater landforms are together called submarine relief or ocean relief.
They include underwater mountains, valleys, plateaus and trenches.
Ocean water is always in motion; its movements shape the surface, support marine life, aid fishing and influence climate.
slides.note: Samundar ke neeche poori duniya basi hai!

slides.title: Record Holders of Deep
slides.kicker: Deeper than Everest is tall, meet the champions
bullets: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth.
The Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range, hidden beneath the ocean.
Some underwater mountains, like Mauna Kea in Hawai'i, are even taller than Mount Everest.

items: Mariana Trench: deepest spot on Earth

slides.note: Everest ko bhi peechhe chhod diya!

slides.title: From Coast to Deep
slides.kicker: Follow the seafloor as it slopes into darkness
bullets: The continental shelf is the submerged, shallow edge of a continent, rich in marine life and resources like oil and gas.
The continental slope is the steep slope marking the true edge of a continent.
The abyssal plain is the vast, flat and deep ocean floor.
slides.note: Shelf shallow, plain gehra — yaad rakho.

slides.title: Trenches, Seamounts, Guyots
slides.kicker: Flat-topped secrets sculpted by waves over millennia
bullets: Ocean trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean.
Seamounts are underwater mountains, usually of volcanic origin, that rise from the ocean floor but do not reach the sea surface.
Guyots are flat-topped underwater mountains: former seamounts eroded by wave action and later submerged.
slides.note: Same mountain, two avatars!

slides.title: What Makes a Wave
slides.kicker: Wind writes, water dances, energy travels far
bullets: When the surface of the ocean rises and falls alternately, the movement is called a wave.
Waves are primarily caused by winds blowing across the water.
Waves carry energy across the oceans over long distances.
slides.note: Crest upar, trough neeche.

slides.title: Measuring a Wave
slides.kicker: Crests, troughs and the simple math of rhythm
bullets: A crest is the high peak of a wave and a trough is the lower valley between crests.
Wavelength is the horizontal distance between two consecutive wave crests or troughs.
Wave frequency is the number of wave crests passing point A each second.
Wave period is the time required for the wave crest at point A to reach point B.
slides.note: Naap lo, samajh aayega.

slides.title: Waves, Coastal Architects
slides.kicker: One headland, five amazing landforms to explore
bullets: Waves are often called coastal architects as they shape the shoreline through erosion and sediment transport.
Wave action creates erosional features such as sea cracks, caves, arches, sea stacks and stumps.
Waves also form depositional features such as beaches.
slides.note: Beach bhi inka gift hai.

slides.title: Storms and Giant Tsunamis
slides.kicker: When the sea turns angry, know its heights
bullets: During storms, strong winds can generate huge waves that may cause significant damage along coastlines.
Giant waves caused majorly by underwater earthquakes are called tsunamis, and they can be extremely destructive.
The maximum vertical height a tsunami reaches above sea level on the shore is called the run-up height.
Run-up heights can reach up to 30 metres, or even more in extreme cases.

right.title: Tsunamis
items: Run-up height up to 30 metres or more

slides.note: 10 manzilon jitni oonchai socho!

slides.title: The Sea Breathes Twice
slides.kicker: High tide, low tide, twice every single day
bullets: Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water that occur twice a day in most parts of the world.
At high tide (flood tide), the water rises to its highest level and covers much of the shore.
At low tide (ebb tide), the water falls to its lowest level and moves away from the shore.
slides.note: Samundar ki saans, din mein do baar.

slides.title: Spring Tides Explained
slides.kicker: Sun, Moon and Earth standing in one line
bullets: Spring tides occur when the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are aligned in a straight line, on full moon and new moon days.
The combined gravitational pull of the Sun and the Moon causes high tides of unusual heights and low tides that are unusually lower.
Water bulges on opposite sides of the Earth due to this strong gravitational pull.

items: Sun, Earth and Moon line up
Very high highs and very low lows

slides.note: Yahan spring ka matlab mausam nahi hai.

slides.title: Neap Tides Explained
slides.kicker: Moon at quarter phase, two pulls tug apart
bullets: Neap tides occur when the Moon is in its first-quarter and third-quarter phases.
The gravitational pull of the Sun and the Moon acts in different directions.
As a result, the difference between high tide and low tide becomes smaller, producing neap tides.
slides.note: Do raste, kam dum.

slides.title: Tides Help Ships Sail
slides.kicker: Gulf of Khambhat and its twelve-metre tidal drama
bullets: High tides are important for navigation because they raise the water level near the shore, allowing ships to enter harbours more easily.
Tidal information is essential in ports and coastal areas, as tidal ranges in some ports can reach 4-5 metres.
The Gulf of Khambhat has one of the highest tidal ranges, at about 12 metres.
slides.note: Ship aane se pehle tide check karna zaroori.

slides.title: Rivers in the Ocean
slides.kicker: Rivers in the ocean flowing in definite directions
bullets: Ocean currents are continuous streams of water that flow across the ocean surface in definite directions.
They arise from winds, the Earth's rotation (Coriolis force), temperature and salinity differences, and basin shapes.
Currents flowing from warmer regions are called warm currents, while those flowing from colder regions are called cold currents.
slides.note: Coriolis force is Earth's twist.

slides.title: Warm in Red, Cold Blue
slides.kicker: Read any currents map like a true pro
bullets: On maps, warm currents are usually shown in red and cold currents in blue.
Warm currents flow from warmer regions towards cooler areas.
Cold currents flow from colder regions towards warmer areas.
Think about it: these currents affect the temperature of nearby coastal regions.
slides.note: Laal garam, neela thanda.

slides.title: Gulf Stream vs Labrador
slides.kicker: One current warms Norway, another freezes Canada
bullets: The Gulf Stream is a warm current from the Gulf of Mexico; it flows towards Norway and keeps waters relatively warm.
Because of the Gulf Stream, sea ice does not form easily in the Norwegian region despite its high latitude of 60-70 degrees.
The Labrador Current is a cold current flowing along the east coast of Canada, carrying freezing water.
It supports the formation of sea ice and icebergs even at lower latitudes.
slides.note: Ek garam, ek barfi — dono Atlantic mein.

slides.title: Where Currents Meet
slides.kicker: Where two currents meet, fish gather in crowds
bullets: The regions where warm and cold currents meet are known as fishing grounds.
These waters are rich in nutrients.
The nutrients support a large variety of fish, making these regions important fishing grounds.
slides.note: Do currents ki mulaqaat, machhliyon ka mela.

slides.title: Cyclones and Tsunamis
slides.kicker: Two sudden guests arrive from an angry ocean
bullets: Oceans and seas can give rise to sudden natural hazards such as cyclones and tsunamis.
A cyclone is a large rotating storm.
A tsunami is a giant wave caused by earthquakes.
slides.note: Hazards aate hain, par hum taiyaar hain.

slides.title: Early Warning Systems
slides.kicker: A giant alarm system guarding the coastline
bullets: Early Warning Systems work like giant alarm systems for coastal areas.
They help detect cyclones and tsunamis, predict disasters, and issue timely warnings.
Warnings let people evacuate and stay safe; people, communities and governments must act in advance to reduce risks.
slides.note: Alert aaya? Turant safe jagah pahuncho.

slides.title: India's Safety Shield
slides.kicker: NCRMP, DSS, SSEWS: names that protect the coast
bullets: India has Cyclone Warning Services and Marine Weather Services that monitor storms along both the eastern and western coasts.
The NCRMP builds cyclone shelters, strengthens warnings and improves emergency response in cyclone-prone areas.
NCRMP includes a Decision Support System (DSS) for disaster management authorities.
INCOIS, with the IMD, set up the Storm Surge Early Warning System (SSEWS) to forecast cyclone-induced storm surges and coastal inundation.
slides.note: Tayyari pehle, suraksha hamesha.

slides.title: Folklore and GEMINI
slides.kicker: Grandmother's tales plus satellites equal saved lives
bullets: Most deaths during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami occurred in Indonesia, yet the island of Simeulue was largely spared.
Local folklore passed down through generations helped Simeulue residents recognise the warning signs of a tsunami and respond quickly.
GEMINI is a handheld device for fishermen; it receives satellite information and transmits it to mobile phones through Bluetooth.
slides.note: Kahaaniyan bhi jaan bacha sakti hain.

examples.title: Ordering the ocean floor
examples.problem: A ship leaves the coast of a continent and sails towards the deep ocean. Which submarine relief features will it cross, in order, and which of them is rich in marine life and resources like oil and gas?
steps: Recall the main features from coast to deep: continental shelf, continental slope, continental rise and abyssal plain.
The shelf is the submerged, shallow edge of the continent, so it comes first.
Next the floor drops steeply along the continental slope, the true edge of the continent.
The gentle continental rise then leads to the vast, flat and deep abyssal plain.
examples.answer: The ship crosses the continental shelf, then the continental slope, then the continental rise, and finally the abyssal plain. The continental shelf is rich in marine life and resources like oil and gas.

examples.title: Reading tides from the Moon
examples.problem: It is a full moon day and a fishing boat wants to enter a harbour. What kind of tides can be expected, why, and how would they differ on a first-quarter moon day?
steps: On a full moon day, the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are aligned in a straight line.
Their combined gravitational pull causes high tides of unusual heights and unusually lower low tides: spring tides.
High tide raises the water level near the shore, so ships can enter harbours more easily.
On a first-quarter moon day, the Sun and Moon pull in different directions, so the high-low difference shrinks, producing neap tides.
examples.answer: Expect spring tides with unusually high highs and unusually low lows on the full moon day; a first-quarter moon brings neap tides with a smaller difference between high and low tide.

examples.title: One coast freezes, one does not
examples.problem: Norway lies at 60-70 degrees latitude, yet sea ice does not form easily there, while the east coast of Canada sees sea ice and icebergs even at lower latitudes. Explain this using ocean currents.
steps: The Gulf Stream is a warm current originating in the Gulf of Mexico in the Atlantic Ocean.
It flows towards Norway and keeps its waters relatively warm, so sea ice does not form easily despite the high latitude.
The Labrador Current is a cold current flowing along the east coast of Canada, carrying freezing water.
It supports the formation of sea ice and icebergs even at lower latitudes.
examples.answer: Warm currents like the Gulf Stream keep coasts relatively warm, while cold currents like the Labrador Current carry freezing water, so sea ice and icebergs form along Canada's east coast.

examples.title: From headland to stump
examples.problem: Waves constantly attack a headland. Describe, step by step, how erosion finally turns it into a stump.
steps: Hydraulic action opens up a large crack in the headland.
Hydraulic action and abrasion turn the crack into a sea cave, which gets larger.
The back of the cave is eroded through to form a sea arch.
The top of the arch collapses due to gravity, leaving a tall stack of rock.
Over time the stack gets eroded and weathered, forming a stump.
examples.answer: Crack, then sea cave, then arch, then sea stack, and finally a stump.
